newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Timber firm Gotvil to seek JSE listing in a year.
newsitem.headline: Timber firm Gotvil to seek JSE listing in a year.

text.p: International timber group Gotvil Timber said on Friday it was investing 560 million in expanding its African timber operations and would seek a listing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) within a year.

Funds raised from the listing would be used to build a timber by-product industry in South Africa, employing about 3,000 people, and to purchase equipment from the local industry for use in other Africa-based concessions.
"A listing for the Johannesburg Stock Exchange is planned for within one year," Gotvil chairman Gil Gotfried told Reuters.
He said 360 million rand of its investment was financed by Standard Corporate and Merchant Bank, a unit of Standard Bank Investment Corporation.
Some 136 million rand of this amount had been spent on the purchase of South African-sourced equipment for its Democratic Republic of Congo operations.
Negotiations were under way with the South African Reserve Bank to have the group's African assets domiciled in South Africa.
He said Africa now accounted for the bulk of its timber supplies to its export markets in the Far East and Europe.

"The worldwide shortage of hardwood resources has meant that inevitably we would become highly focussed on Africa where some of the last concessions are available," Gotfried said at the launch of its new head office in Sandton, north of Johannesburg.
Gotvil has concessions of over 1.5 million hectares of forest throughout Africa with one million hectare concessions in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

The Congo concession, which accounted for 60 percent of its Africa concession with the balance in Guinea and Madasgascar, remained secure despite current uncertainty and doubts about the government's willingness to honour existing contracts.

Gotvil said it intended to further expand its operations in Africa despite political worries prevailing and was negotiating with the Mozambican government to secure 200,000 to 500,000 hectare forestry concessions.
It was also planning to build a wood processing plant in Mozambique, with the initial stage costing $35 million.
Gotvil is primarily a trading and export company and sells the entirety of its production to mills in Japan, the Far East and Europe where mill prices are substantially higher than South Africa.
It said it did not intend to compete with local producers Sappi Ltd and Mondi, who were primarily in softwood production, and did minimal beneficiation of its hardwood production.

"We expect to achieve a turnover of 1.8 billion rand in our financial year ending in 1998, which will be exported to our traditional markets. There is such a scarcity of hardwood that there is no problem selling our production," Gotfried said.
Gotvil was started in Russia in 1903 and spread through Eastern Europe and established its head office in London which has now been relocated to Johannesburg.
